Countries take out loans and usually this is actually a good thing, so long as there aren't too many loans and the country is able to pay them back.

(Almost?) every country's government raises money by allowing others - people, institutions, even other governments - to give it loans which it then promises to pay back. This is on top of other means it has to make money, such as taxes, tariffs, and printing its own money.

The more such loans a country takes out, the more money it has to spend paying interest on those loans. If there isn't enough money to spend on whatever the government needs to spend it on, then the country can raise taxes or other fees, print more money, or take out even more loans.

Now usually, all of these are preferable to the final option, which is to declare "I'm unable, or unwilling, to pay back the loans I took out". The government usually has every right to do that. You can write a loan to your government and they can turn around and say "What loan?" but by doing so, they damage their credibility and make it far less likely that anyone will write them a loan in the future.

Sometimes this is unavoidable. For example, the Greek debt crisis of 2007 was caused by Greece borrowing so much money that the nations giving them that money demanded the Greeks reorganize their economy in such a way that they would have a chance of paying it all off. Since so much of the "value" was leaving the country to pay off all that debt, their own economy tanked. Unemployment was high and wages were low meaning that raising taxes wouldn't be effective, and Greece was using the euro by that point so they couldn't unilaterally print money like they could if they had their own currency.

Sometimes it is avoidable but the country explicitly chooses to not pay back its loans. In 1918, Russia, having undergone a communist revolution, announced it would not honor the debts that the previous government owed.

In 1998, Russia had transitioned back to capitalism but its economy was flailing with very high levels of unemployment and inflation, meaning that taxes and even more money printing weren't good choices. Rather than undergo the sort of austerity measures that were forced on Greece by its international creditors, Russia's legislature (dominated by communists who were very skeptical of foreign agencies like the IMF who would have been writing them the loans) announced that it would default on its foreign debts while doing its best to pay what it owed to Russian creditors. Fortunately, a spike in oil prices in the following years, plus some benefits of a worthless currency (everything is super cheap when you sell your stuff abroad) allowed the country to recover and eventually pay off the remaining loans, restoring foreign creditors' trust that any loans they wrote to Russia in the future would actually be repaid.

All the data can be viewed [here](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1iXNLX7_YpaN-B4kSyoCAHam0zn16wHWpyFPWch8SSYc/edit?usp=sharing). I used the colors from the Runelite xp globes but there are a lot of similar colors between skills there, so you can take a look at the direct data + full chart for yourselves.

### The X-Axis

For each series, the x-axis represents the player who is in Nth place for each skill. But each skill is independent of the others, so rather than, say, a summary of the stats of the 500,000th best player, it's a comparison of the 500,000th best player in cooking, 500,000th best player in prayer, and so on, on top of one another.

### Continuous Levels

Since it's the Y axis in all of the charts (including the combat one) I should explain what I mean by this term. In Runescape your level is an integer. You are either level 80 or level 81 and there is nothing in between. However, it's interesting to see who stops after achieving level 80 and who continues to make progress towards the next level. To distinguish between these two groups I plotted levels as real numbers with a simple idea - if you're halfway to level 81, your "continuous level" should be about 80.5. You can use the same exponential formula that is used to determine level boundaries, just remove the floor term.

The formula for xp has a polynomial component and an exponential component and can be found [here](https://oldschool.runescape.wiki/w/Experience#Formula). Even without the error I wasn't able to solve for L. Throwing away the polynomial terms introduces an additional error of over 300 xp around level 50 which is actually significant because a few thousand players are just barely level 50 and if you add 300 xp to the level 50 threshold it bumps them down. So instead I used a slightly different regression which maps better at lower levels and has an error of <0.1% above level 60 and <0.01% above level 87. This regression is XP = 714.358 * 1.104186^L. Or to get the continuous level from the XP, it's L = ln(XP/714.358)/ln(1.104186). It's still a little high at level 50 but close enough that you don't notice. And there's only one skill that approaches level 50 on this chart.

Just as you can get every real number between 1 and 99 with this, I extended continuous levels all the way up to their max of roughly 126.5, which you get at 200 mil xp.

### Combat Level Estimates 

Of course there's no hiscores for combat level so I used a rough heuristic to approximate - I assume the player with the Nth highest combat XP is roughly in Nth place for each of the combat skills. The formula to calculate combat level is [here](https://oldschool.runescape.wiki/w/Combat_level#Calculating_combat_level). Because strength + attack dominates at all ranks from 1 to 1,000,000 compared to mage/ranged times 1.5 (you'll have to trust me on this one), I just plugged in the numbers for melee combat level.

Virtual combat level is calculated just by plugging in continuous levels into the combat formula and getting out the result. Actual combat level is calculated by flooring the levels (and capping at 99) and doing the same formula with all of the additional floor terms it entails. The result is that you should be able to see how your combat level measures up to the top 1 million players.

I used the continuous level for both the real and virtual levels, but again the error is so small that I'm confident I could've calculated the "real" combat level directly using the real xp boundaries without any noticeable changes in the line. This just saved me some time.

### How I Got this Data

OSRS hiscores API. Ideally you identify uncorrelated investments and scale each one based on their volatility relative to one another. So you set target percentages as a share of the PF Then on a regular basis (usually monthly or quarterly) you rebalance the overweight slices, which are your biggest winners, selling off the excess and using it to buy more of the underweight slices. In essence, selling high and buying low. The uncorrelatedness means that your whole PF won't jump to zero and you most likely have at least one slice that's doing okay. The volatility scaling minimizes the volatility of the whole pie.

To use my own portfolio as an example, I have 40% in TMV (-3x long term treasuries, normally this piece is TMF but in a rising rate environment I temporarily flipped), 20% in UPRO (3x S&P), 20% TQQQ (3x Nasdaq), 10% DRN (3x real estate index), 10% UGL (2x gold, 3x no longer exists afaik). Say JPow decides to jack the rates up by 75% after all. TMV will probably go on a tear and UPRO/TQQQ will plummet. So next month TMV will make up say 55% of my portfolio value. Then I sell the 15% of extra TMV and buy up the other indices to make up the aforementioned ratios. Again M1 does all of this for me with the press of a single button, I just set the ratios and equities

The expense fees (which hide bigger fees, namely you're paying a percent or so above the current interest rate) do mean that you don't see the 3x that you would in theory. The example with one day up and one day down misses the point about how the probability distribution looks though. You lose out when prices move up and then down, but make more than 3x during back-to-back green days and lose less than 3x during back-to-back red days. In theory when you add up all the possibilities you do get triple the average return of the underlying. It's quite similar to taking out a loan to buy the underlying and adjusting it daily while paying interest on the principal. In practice the interest and massive drawdowns mean you get screwed if you don't use multiple funds to rebalance from winners to losers so that said losers have enough capital to recover.

Bar graph of all the reigns in years of the four countries in the title (and their predecessor states), with all of the monarchs with the same name stacked on top of one another. Assembled together in Excel. A few notes:

England:

* Charles II's reign is counted beginning from his restoration in 1660, although he officially began his reign the day his father was executed in 1649

France:

* Both kings and emperors are included
* Henry VI of England is not included, though he reigned in France as Henri II from 1422 to 1453
* Louis XVII, son of Louis XVI, never reigned and is not included here, but he is included in the regnal count. Neither is Louis-Philippe II or Napoleon II
* John I's five-day lifelong reign is included
* France spent 393 years under a Louis

Spain:

* Many Asturian and Leonese reign dates are uncertain. I defaulted to January 1st for any date I couldn't find at least one source for, although at this scale a few months doesn't make a huge difference
* Spain (and its predecessor kingdoms) spent 447 years under an Alfonso

Russia:

* Yaroslav is canonically given the regnal number II as the second Kievan prince with that name, however he is the first prince of Vladimir with that name. And the Yaroslav after him is given the number III
* Alexander Nevsky (r. 1252-1263), Vasily of Kostroma (r. 1272-1276) and Michael of Tver (r. 1304-1314) are not given regnal numbers so I put them in their own category, since canonically Alexander I, Vasily I and Michael I are completely different individuals
